items.item: single-flight coalescing is measured reducing many concurrent readers' backing-store fetches on a hot key down to one, and early expiration's refresh probability is measured rising as a key nears its TTL

The delete-after-write race is not a bug in delete-on-write; it is a timing problem that delete-on-write alone cannot close, because the delete and the reader's own slow write-back can land in either order regardless of which write-path operation is used.

at.step: Hook: a reader's stale read lands in the cache right after a writer already deleted that key

items.item: Update is strictly riskier than delete here, not merely equally risky: two concurrent updates can land in either order and silently overwrite a newer value with an older one, a failure mode two concurrent deletes cannot produce since they always leave the same cold result.

A lease closes the race by binding a token to the specific read that caused the miss, so a delete that happens after that token was issued can invalidate exactly that reader's own pending write-back, without needing to know anything else about which value is stale.

CDC-driven invalidation and leases solve two different problems, not the same one twice: leases arbitrate a specific race between one reader's write-back and one writer's delete, while CDC-driven invalidation guarantees every write path's delete actually gets sent at all, regardless of whether that write path remembered to call anything.

Per-field staleness is a routing decision, not a different storage engine: the same TAO store serves both an eventually consistent read and a critical one, differing only in which copy the request is proxied to, not in what the data model is.

at.step: Reveal: per-field staleness, the TAO case study

items.item: Single-flight coalescing and leases both reduce concurrent work on a miss, but for different reasons: coalescing exists to avoid redundant backing-store load from many simultaneous misses on the same key, while a lease exists to arbitrate which of several concurrent writers is allowed to actually set the value — a cache can need either without the other.

Early expiration's probability curve is deliberately smooth rather than a step function at the exact TTL boundary, because a step function at one instant is exactly what recreates a thundering herd — every reader checking at that instant would refresh simultaneously, which is the failure the smooth curve is built to avoid.

This topic's own CDC-driven-invalidation reveal depends directly on the prior chapter's own physical-vs-logical-replication material: mcsqueal's daemon is reading the same kind of commit-log stream that topic 18's logical replication already introduced, applied here to cache invalidation instead of replica catch-up.

This topic establishes that a cache's contents can be kept correct under concurrent writes; it says nothing yet about what internals make a real cache engine (eviction, persistence, replication) actually behave this way, which is exactly the gap the next topic closes by naming one real engine directly.

The hook's own race is strictly worse than ordinary staleness: an ordinary stale cache entry self-corrects on its own TTL or next write, but the delete-after-write race can leave a cache holding a stale value indefinitely, with nothing left in the system that will ever trigger a correction on its own.
